text:
Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.
The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.
In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.
Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model. The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.
In theory, according to diplomatic sources, migrants would stay in a reception centre in Rwanda for a couple of months, before choosing to integrate into life in the Great Lakes country or return to their home nation.
Unlike the failed scheme pursued by the British Conservative government in Rwanda, or Italy’s agreement with Albania, it will not apply to people pursuing asylum claims.
The reception centre, which would be an open facility, is not intended to house people in the long-term, but accommodate regular flows of people. Diplomatic sources said the EU countries were not using the British-funded facilities built in Kigali.
The governments involved argue that it will protect the European asylum system while removing the incentive for irregular migrants to come to Europe.
Denmark’s immigration minister Morten Bødskov, whose government has pioneered a tough line on migration widely emulated across the EU, said today was “a huge breakthrough”.
German interior minister Alexander Dobrindt said: “Return hubs offer a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe, whose countries of origin do not co-operate in the repatriation process.”
Andy Burnham told reporters last week that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that with interest, learning from what went on in the past. The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”
Critics have highlighted the ethics of striking an agreement with Rwanda’s repressive government, which was found in 2024 by the US State Department to allow state security forces and civilian officials to commit human rights abuses with impunity, while also raising concerns about freedom of expression and forced labour.
French Green MEP Mélissa Camara, a long-term critic, denounced the agreement between the five countries and Rwanda as “an agreement of shame” and “a grave moral failing”. She said: “Under this agreement, people will be deported thousands of kilometres away from the European Union, with no guarantees regarding the compliance with their rights”.
Alain Berset, the secretary-general of the Council of Europe, the continent’s human rights body, said it was not possible “to be so precise a priori” about what any return hubs proposals meant. Speaking to the Guardian before the announcement, he said all members of the Council of Europe were committed to the European Convention on Human Rights “and this must be the lighthouse” for all discussions on return hubs
“On concrete cases, then we will have to see if this is compliant with the convention,” he said, adding that there was no “one or zero logic”. He stressed that “all countries must be able to define their migration policy”.
Officials involve in setting up the migration centres expect legal challenges, but argue the scheme is grounded in human-rights law.
Rights organisations argue the scheme will fail, as people will seek to move on to be close to family and friends. “Member states may call them ‘return hubs’ or even ‘welcome centres’, but no euphemism can hide the violence of uprooting people from the life they’ve been building in Europe, and sending them to a country they don’t even know, without family, networks or meaningful prospects,” said Chiara Catelli of Picum, a pan-European organisation that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants.
